title: Thu phí ùn tắc · Discuss both views
prompt: Some people support charging drivers to enter congested city centres, while others oppose it because of the risks it could create. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

paragraphs: Congestion charges make drivers confront the cost of occupying scarce city-centre road space. I support congestion charging as a priority where revenue expands usable public transport and narrowly drawn exemptions protect essential journeys without alternatives.

Supporters argue that congestion charging can make scarce road space work more efficiently. A charge encourages flexible journeys to move to other times or modes, leaving space for essential traffic. A commuter with a frequent rail connection might stop driving into the centre. Some drivers changing flexible journeys can improve road conditions for those who still need to drive, so the benefit is not limited to people who switch modes.

Opponents warn that people working unsocial hours may have no realistic alternative to driving. Travellers with fixed hours and no suitable public service cannot easily change their route or departure time. They may continue driving and absorb the charge, so the policy's financial burden can fall on essential journeys rather than only discourage flexible or unnecessary traffic. Revenue should improve transport coverage and provide narrowly defined exemptions. Better coverage expands alternatives, while narrowly defined exemptions recognise necessity without allowing so many free entries that congestion simply returns. Authorities should map early and late shifts against service timetables before setting exemptions, because a bus route on a map is not an alternative if its last departure precedes the worker's shift. Small changes across many flexible journeys can save considerable travel time, but charging workers who cannot switch modes creates hardship without the same behavioural benefit.
In conclusion, charging can improve crowded roads when it changes avoidable travel; its legitimacy also depends on protecting necessary journeys and using revenue to widen realistic alternatives.
